title: What is a stack: a box where you can only add/remove from the TOP (Last In First Out: LIFO), like a stack of plates.
keyPoints: A stack is a linear LIFO data structure where push, pop, and peek all run in O(1) time.
Use ArrayDeque as your stack in Java instead of the legacy synchronized Stack class.
The JVM call stack uses LIFO ordering for method frames, which is why infinite recursion throws StackOverflowError.
Stacks power undo features, balanced-bracket validation, expression evaluation, and DFS traversal.
Always check isEmpty() before calling pop() or peek() to avoid NoSuchElementException.
A stack provides no indexed access; you can only interact with the element on top.

s1_definition.oneliner: A stack is Last In First Out: you only add and remove from the top, like a pile of plates.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Stack** – a linear data structure that follows Last In First Out (LIFO) ordering, meaning the most recently added element is always the first one removed.
- **push** – places a new element on top of the stack in O(1) time.
- **pop** – removes and returns the current top element in O(1) time.
- **peek** – returns the top element without removing it in O(1) time.
- **isEmpty** – checks whether the stack contains zero elements.
- **ArrayDeque** – the recommended Java implementation for a stack, preferred over the legacy `Stack` class because it is not synchronized and does not expose vector methods that break the stack abstraction.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a pile of transaction receipts on Rajesh's desk at the National Bank of India. Every time a customer completes a deposit, Rajesh places the receipt on top of the pile. When the auditor asks for the latest receipt, Rajesh picks up the one on top, which is always the most recent. He cannot pull a receipt from the middle without first removing every receipt above it. That pile of receipts is exactly a stack.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A stack is a linear data structure that follows Last In First Out ordering. The most recently added element always sits on top, and it is the first one removed. The three core operations, push, pop, and peek, all run in constant time, and there is deliberately no way to reach into the middle. That restriction is exactly what makes a stack so predictable and so useful for problems where the latest item must be handled first.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used a stack to implement an undo feature for the account management console. As Rajesh performs actions like adding a payee, setting a transfer limit, or scheduling a payment, each action is pushed onto the stack. When he taps undo, the top action is popped, which is always the most recent one, and the actions are reversed in exactly the order users expect. Without the LIFO guarantee, undo would not feel natural.

In modern Java, I always use `ArrayDeque` as my stack rather than the legacy `Stack` class. The old `Stack` extends `Vector`, which synchronizes every call and exposes indexed-access methods that let callers reach into the middle and break the LIFO contract. `ArrayDeque` avoids both problems and is measurably faster. I also always check `isEmpty()` before calling pop or peek, because an empty `ArrayDeque` throws `NoSuchElementException`, and I want the code to handle the empty case gracefully rather than crashing.

The JVM itself uses a stack for method calls: each thread has a call stack where a frame is pushed on method entry and popped on return. That is why infinite recursion produces a `StackOverflowError` rather than running forever. Understanding this connection between the data structure and the runtime helps explain why stacks appear everywhere in computing, from expression evaluation to depth-first search to backtracking.

Remember one sentence: a stack is Last In First Out, where push, pop, and peek all run in O(1) and the top element is always the most recently added.
